analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 Bush tax cuts permanent instead of letting them expire.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the 107th Congress ended, with 115 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The big 2001 tax law (the Bush tax cuts) was written with a built-in expiration date: its rate cuts, child tax credit increase, marriage-penalty relief, and estate tax repeal all phase back out after 2010. This bill would strike that expiration date, locking in every 2001 tax cut permanently. The bill was sent to the House tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest and most permanent gains would go to the wealthiest households: full repeal of the estate tax affects only the largest estates, and the top income-rate cuts and capital gains provisions deliver the biggest dollar benefits to high earners. Middle- and lower-income families would also keep the expanded child tax credit, marriage-penalty relief, and the earned income tax credit expansion that the 2001 law contained, and businesses and investors would keep lower tax rates on income and gains.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the section of the 2001 tax law that makes all of its provisions expire, so the rate cuts, child credit expansion, marriage-penalty relief, and estate tax phase-out would never phase back out.
The bill's own subject list includes estate and inheritance tax repeal, which directly benefits the owners of large estates and closely held businesses.
The bill also makes permanent the law's expanded earned income tax credit and education savings provisions, which help lower- and middle-income working families.

analysis.who_pays: The tax cuts cost the federal treasury revenue; making them permanent means that revenue loss never ends, so the cost is a permanently larger deficit unless future Congresses cut spending or raise other taxes. Future taxpayers, and programs competing for federal dollars, bear that cost. The distribution of the original cuts means the richest households pay the least relative to what they receive.

drawbacks.text: Making all of the 2001 tax cuts permanent without any offsetting revenue would permanently increase federal deficits, since the cuts were originally sized to fit a ten-year window precisely because they were scheduled to end.

The benefits are heavily skewed upward: estate tax repeal matters only to the largest estates, and the rate and capital gains provisions deliver the largest dollar amounts to the highest-income households, while the lost revenue affects everyone.

Because the bill simply strikes the sunset section, it locks in the 2001 law exactly as written, including its phase-in schedule and any provisions critics considered poorly designed, with no reexamination of whether each piece was worth its cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Keeping the child tax credit and earned income tax credit expansions permanent is a genuine benefit to working families, and tax certainty has real value. But the bill is a blunt instrument: it makes every 2001 provision permanent, and the largest dollar benefits flow to the top of the income scale and to large estates, while the cost is a permanent hole in federal revenue. A bill that extended only the provisions helping working families would have captured most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Kenny Hulshof introduced the bill on June 26, 2001.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further steps of any kind.
The bill attracted 115 cosponsors, 113 of the 223 House Republicans and 2 of the 208 House Democrats.
The bill's sole effect was to repeal the section of the 2001 tax law that makes its provisions expire.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 2001 tax cuts kept their scheduled expiration, so the fiscal cost of making them permanent was never locked in, and large estates did not get permanent repeal. The committee that never acted, and the tax cuts' sunset date, were what mattered; supporters could claim cosponsorship without the bill ever facing scrutiny or a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal balance sheet, not large estates

for.name: Kenny Hulshof
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 tax cuts permanent.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor action, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 113 of 223 House Republicans cosigned versus 2 of 208 House Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote where the split could be measured.

industries.note: Permanent estate tax repeal and top-rate cuts deliver the largest dollar benefits to the top of the income scale, while the lost revenue must be made up by deficits or by future tax and spending changes that fall on everyone.
The bill locks in permanently lower taxes on capital income and gains, a benefit concentrated among households that own substantial investments.

industries.industry: Closely held businesses and family farms
industries.note: Permanent estate tax repeal would spare heirs of family businesses and farms from estate taxes; the benefit is real but flows mainly to larger operations.
Full permanent repeal of the estate tax removes much of the business built around structuring estates to limit tax exposure.
